title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
content:
Replit CEO and co-founder, Amjad Masad, has seen how AI is impacting the workplace first-hand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.
He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste.
“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.
“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”
Illustrating the shift, the Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.
“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.
“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”
He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said).
“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

report.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad predicts AI agents will create 'self-driving companies,' automating grunt work while humans focus on judgment, taste, and deciding what to build.
report.background: Over the past year, AI coding assistants have evolved from autocomplete tools into autonomous agents capable of triaging issues, editing codebases, and opening patches. Replit, founded as a browser-based coding platform, has ridden that shift, with businesses using its AI tools to build and ship software faster. CEO Amjad Masad’s remarks at TechCrunch Disrupt reflect a broader Silicon Valley debate: as agents become more reliable, will they replace workers or reshape what workers do? Replit says its own operations changed after agents improved, prompting the 'self-driving company' metaphor. The vision contrasts with dystopian automation narratives, arguing that human judgment, taste, and prioritization remain essential. It also arrives as enterprises experiment with agentic workflows across support, engineering, and operations, seeking productivity gains amid pressure to do more with existing teams.
key_points: Masad describes a self-driving company as one where AI agents handle repetitive work and keep processes moving, while humans step in for judgment. At Replit, support tickets are first triaged by an agent that reviews GitHub issues, codebase context, and Linear tickets. A human then decides the fix, and another agent helps deploy it. The loop is automated but not autonomous.

The CEO argues agents are not mainly eliminating jobs; they are changing job content. Replit employees spend more time deciding what to build, debating architecture, and whiteboarding. Masad says this shift makes work less boring and more creative, because people focus on problems that require taste and strategic thinking rather than routine execution.

Masad warns the change will surprise many workers outside tech hubs. While Disrupt attendees may already feel AI reshaping their roles, much of America and the world has not yet experienced it. He frames the coming transition as broad and disruptive, not limited to software engineers, and says companies need a positive vision for how AI improves work.

Replit’s internal workflow shows the model in practice: an agent does initial investigation, a human applies judgment, and an agent executes the fix. Masad insists human judgment and taste are not going away soon. The company is also telling other businesses that AI should make employees more productive and happier, not just cheaper.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Masad’s 'self-driving company' is a product roadmap and a narrative counterpoint to job-replacement fears: agentic workflows that keep humans in the loop. Developers may see their roles shift toward architecture, review, and orchestration—less boilerplate, more judgment—while needing skills to manage agents, write clear specs, and evaluate output. Regular users could get faster support and software built by smaller teams, but also face opaque automated decisions and new accountability questions. Enterprises will likely adopt triage-and-deploy loops first, where ROI is measurable. The risk is that if agents handle most execution, junior hiring and traditional apprenticeship paths could shrink, concentrating expertise among those who already have taste and context.
report.tools: To follow this trend, watch Replit Agent and Replit Teams for the commercial workflow Masad describes. Developers can try open-source coding agents such as OpenHands, SWE-agent, and Aider, or IDE copilots like Cursor, Continue, and GitHub Copilot Workspace. For orchestration, LangGraph, CrewAI, and Microsoft AutoGen help build multi-agent loops with human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Also track Linear and GitHub integrations, since triage across tickets and codebases is central to the self-driving company model.
